nameStory: This tiny clam earned its beautiful name from the lovely purple hues that wash across both the inside and outside of its small shell, reminiscent of the precious amethyst gemstone. The 'gem' part of its name refers both to this purple coloring and its diminutive, jewel-like size that makes each shell a tiny treasure on the beach.
description: The amethyst gem clam is one of New England's tiniest saltwater clams, growing no larger than your pinky nail at just 5 millimeters long. These miniature bivalves have whitish or grayish shells that are beautifully tinted with purple coloring on both the outer shell and the inner mother-of-pearl surface. Despite their small size, they're true clams with the classic two-hinged shell design, living buried in sandy and muddy coastal areas. You'll need to look closely to spot these little gems, as they're easily overlooked among beach debris.

idTips.label: Purple Tinting
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive purple wash or suffusion across the shell surface, visible on both the outside and inside of the shell when opened

idTips.label: Tiny Size
idTips.description: Measures only about 5mm long - roughly the size of a small pea or the tip of your pinky finger

idTips.label: Shell Color Base
idTips.description: Base shell color is whitish to pale gray, providing a soft backdrop for the purple coloring

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Classic clam shape with two rounded, hinged shells that fit tightly together when closed

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth shell surface with a slightly glossy feel when wet, becoming duller when dried

habitat: Look for amethyst gem clams in sandy and muddy areas of salt marshes, tidal flats, and shallow coastal waters throughout New England's coastline. They burrow into soft sediments in protected bays and estuaries where the water is calmer than open ocean beaches. You're most likely to find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, or spot live ones while digging in mudflats during low tide.

seasonality.spring: Shell collecting is good as winter storms wash up specimens on beaches. Live clams become more active in warming sediments.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding live clams during low tide exploration of mudflats and shallow waters. Shells are often found mixed with other beach treasures.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases shell finds on beaches. Clams begin to burrow deeper as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Clams remain buried deep in sediment. Best season for finding shells on storm-washed beaches, though harsh weather limits collecting opportunities.

funFact: Despite being native to the Atlantic coast, amethyst gem clams have somehow hitchhiked their way to the Pacific coast, likely traveling in ship ballast water or on boat hulls - making this tiny purple gem one of the few New England shellfish that has successfully colonized the opposite side of the continent!
confusionNotes: These tiny clams might be confused with young specimens of other small clams, but the distinctive purple coloring on both shell surfaces is unique among New England's coastal clams. Remember: "Purple inside and out = amethyst gem clam, no doubt!"
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Gemma gemma literally means "gem gem," emphasizing just how gem-like early naturalists found these tiny purple treasures. Unlike many clam species that have separate common names from their scientific names, this species' beauty was so striking that both names celebrate its jewel-like qualities.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Gemma found in New England, the amethyst gem clam is quite distinctive. Compared to other small Venus clams in the family Veneridae, it's significantly smaller and is the only one with the characteristic purple tinting on both shell surfaces. Other small clams in the region lack this distinctive amethyst coloration and tend to be larger overall.
